title: Vireo Labs - Customer Spotlight Podcast Recording
summary: A conversational, podcast-style customer interview recording focusing on Vireo Labs' journey integrating Redwood Inference into their clinical triage product. Covers initial evaluation, performance wins, cost tradeoffs, private deployment considerations, and outcomes for their go-to-market. Informal tone; intended for marketing assets and a short case study video.
topics: Why Redwood: latency and reliability needs
Quantitative wins: latency, cost per request
Marketing and go-to-market impact from using Redwood
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hi everyone, welcome to the Redwood Customer Spotlight — I'm Lena in marketing, thanks for joining. Today we're chatting with Vireo Labs about how they're using Redwood for clinical triage. Priya, would you like to kick us off with a quick intro?
[00:14] Dr. Priya Kapoor: Yeah, thanks Lena. Hi, I'm Priya, founder and CEO at Vireo Labs. We build an AI-first pre-triage workflow for hospitals to prioritize incoming cases, so speed and accuracy really matter.
[00:27] Lena Ortiz: Great, and Jonas, can you say a bit about the ML side?
[00:31] Jonas Meyer: Sure. So we're running an ensemble of transformer models for text and structured input, and previously we were on a self-hosted setup that was, uh, fragile — lots of ops overhead. We wanted something that could give us predictable latency under load.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Yeah that's exactly what we chatted about during the POC — the burstiness of hospital traffic makes batching tricky. Did you start with Hosted or Dedicated?
[00:52] Jonas Meyer: We started with Hosted to move fast, then moved to Dedicated reserved nodes after a couple months because of the throughput SLA we needed. The switch was surprisingly smooth.
[01:03] Hannah Lee (customer): From a product standpoint it mattered that we could measure token-level costs — that allowed the finance team to sign off.
[01:10] Lena Ortiz: Love that. Can you describe a specific moment where Redwood changed the way you operate?
[01:16] Dr. Priya Kapoor: Yeah, during flu season we had a 3x traffic spike. Before Redwood, requests piled up, and wait times for triage were minutes. After moving to Dedicated and enabling prefix caching, our 95th percentile latency dropped from ~1.2 s per request to about 220 ms under peak, which is night and day.
[01:33] Ethan Park (Redwood SE): Quick clarification — you mentioned prefix caching, we actually implemented a custom KV cash preference during the rollout — and it leaned into the runtime's continuous batching. There was a mis- — sorry, "KV cash" that the ops team initially called it.
[01:48] Jonas Meyer: (laughs) Yeah the docs had a typo, we called it that in slack for a week. But the caching and batching tuned together was the multiplier.
[01:56] Lena Ortiz: There was also a security angle — Priya, what were the compliance checks you required?
[02:01] Dr. Priya Kapoor: We needed SOC 2 type II evidence, SSO via SAML, and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Redwood's Private deployment and KMS integration were big factors — we run a VPC control plane and manage keys with our cloud KMS. The security review took about three weeks including a short penetration test.
[02:18] Maya Chen: We also provided the SOC package and a short runbook for the penetration test — happy to share that link in the notes.
[02:25] Jonas Meyer: Implementation-wise the onboarding was around four weeks: initial spike test, model variant testing, and then a staged rollout. The SE team helped with kernel selection and quantization tuning; that cut our GPU memory footprint by about 40%.
[02:40] Hannah Lee: From adoption — one metric we love — our internal triage throughput improved by 2.4x which allowed us to take on three additional hospital clients without hiring more ops staff.
[02:51] Lena Ortiz: That's a great outcome. Were there any surprising tradeoffs or things you wish you'd known earlier?
[02:56] Jonas Meyer: I wish we had scoped the eval prompts more conservatively — we saw some regression in edge-case classification when we moved to a heavily quantized model. The Redwood SEs helped set up a regression eval suite which we ran nightly and it caught the drift.
[03:13] Ethan Park: Yeah — the nightly evaluation with a prompt set was something we recommended early but they increased the coverage later which improved confidence.
[03:21] Lena Ortiz: Any competitors you evaluated during selection?
[03:24] Jonas Meyer: We looked at a Hosted option from a major cloud vendor and a smaller inference runtime vendor; the cloud vendor had good integration but the cost per 1k requests was higher and we couldn't get the same level of control over kernels and batching. So cost + performance + security pushed us to Redwood.
[03:42] Dr. Priya Kapoor: Also, the support model mattered. Redwood's SRE-backed support was more responsive during our peak tests.
[03:50] Hannah Lee: For the marketing part of this podcast, what sorts of numbers can we share publicly? The performance delta?
[03:56] Maya Chen: We typically allow high-level numbers: percent latency reduction, throughput increase, cost-per-request improvements. For anything customer-specific like exact hospital names or revenue numbers we'll need sign-off.
[04:08] Dr. Priya Kapoor: We're OK with the aggregate metrics — 95th pctl latency improvement, 2.4x throughput, and roughly 30% reduction in per-request infra cost. Don't publish client names.
[04:18] Lena Ortiz: Noted. Quick technical aside — Jonas, can you explain how you validated model quality after quantization?
[04:24] Jonas Meyer: We had a two-step process: an offline eval set to measure macro metrics, then a canary in production on 5% traffic. The canary used A/B with automatic fallback to the fp16 model if we detected a quality regression beyond a threshold. That automated fallback was super valuable.
[04:40] Ethan Park: And that fallback used routing policies in the control plane so you didn't have to re-deploy.
[04:45] Jonas Meyer: Exactly. Another note — the Redwood console's trace and token cost breakdown helped us tune prompt templates to reduce unnecessary tokens, saving money.
[04:54] Hannah Lee: How about org buy-in — any tips for pitching this internally?
[04:58] Dr. Priya Kapoor: Tie it to SLAs for the hospitals. When you can say "we will triage within X ms" and back it with numbers, procurement signs faster. Also align with security early.
[05:10] Lena Ortiz: Perfect. We're coming up on the end, any final stories or advice?
[05:14] Jonas Meyer: Spend time on model variants, and ramp quantization gradually. Don't assume one setting fits all sequences.
[05:21] Maya Chen: One last plug — if any listeners want the technical checklist we used during the POC, we'll share a lightweight spreadsheet and the SOC packet link.
[05:30] Dr. Priya Kapoor: Happy to say that this partnership let us focus more on product and less on infra; our engineering team can concentrate on edge-case models rather than GPU packing.
[05:40] Lena Ortiz: Amazing, thank you all. We'll cut an edit for a short 12-minute episode and a longer full-length recording for internal use. We'll share the draft copy and ask for approvals.
[05:52] Hannah Lee: Sounds good — please send the share link.
[05:55] Maya Chen: I'll follow up with the SOC link, the POC checklist, and a short excerpt transcript.
[06:02] Lena Ortiz: Thanks everyone — recording stopped.

Note: The transcript above is an edited export from the recorded session. There are small misrecognitions (e.g., "KV cash" for KV cache) and informal asides preserved. Some timestamps correspond to the long-form recording; the marketing edit will remove filler and tighten transitions.
